Article Title: ‘Build new NTA’: Exam body begins major revamp, seeks experts for four senior roles
Article Text:
General Manager, Assessment R&D and Psychometrics

General Manager, Test Centre Network & Operations

General Manager, Information Security (Chief Information Security Officer)

General Manager, Vigilance, Investigation & Forensics

The National Testing Agency NTA ) has begun a major leadership overhaul as it moves to rebuild its examination framework, strengthen security systems and restore confidence in the country's competitive examination process.As part of its "Build New NTA" initiative, the testing body has invited applications for four senior leadership roles focused on assessment, operations, cyber security and investigation.The revamp comes amid months of protests over the alleged NEET paper leak, which led to demands for accountability and the resignation of then education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The Centre has since announced a series of measures to strengthen examination systems, including the introduction of an anti-paper leak law and the establishment of fast-track courts to hear related cases.In a LinkedIn post announcing the recruitment drive, the NTA said, "We are hiring for four senior leadership roles. And we are looking for the best India has to offer."The agency said the initiative was aimed at rebuilding an institution that conducts examinations affecting millions of students every year."Every year, more than 1 crore young Indians take a National Testing Agency examination," the NTA said.It added that the future of candidates depends on the "integrity, fairness and quality" of its examination process, as the results influence their education, careers and future opportunities.Emphasising the need for reform, the agency wrote, "It is a responsibility we take very seriously. And it is a responsibility we are rebuilding NTA to be worthy of."The NTA said the restructuring exercise follows the recommendations of the High-Level Committee of Experts (HLCE), chaired by K Radhakrishnan.It added, "Across academic rigour, technology, security, operations and governance, we are rebuilding the Agency to serve crores of candidates with the credibility they deserve."As part of the overhaul, the NTA is seeking candidates for four senior positions:The agency said the vigilance and forensics head would oversee investigations into examination malpractice, coordinate with agencies including the CBI, IB, ED and state police, and operate under the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024.The NTA conducts several major entrance examinations, including Neet, Jee and Cuet.Highlighting the broader purpose of the reforms, the NTA said, "The candidates who write NTA examinations are the future of India. They are the engineers who will build our infrastructure, the doctors who will care for our people, the teachers who will educate the next generation, and the researchers who will drive our discovery."The agency has also invited applications for Young Professionals through the UPSC's Pratibha Setu portal, with 12 positions in Academic Research, two in Legal Research and two in Finance & Accounts Research.According to the NTA, applications for the senior leadership positions can be submitted by email to dir-admin@nta.gov.in, with the deadline set at 30 days from July 25, 2026.The recruitment drive notification comes as Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a high-powered committee headed by Nandan Nilekani to recommend measures for leak-proof and technology-driven examinations.Later, home minister Amit Shah said on X, "The Modi govt follows the principle of constant reform to safeguard the future of our new generation."Shah added, "We will impose exemplary punishment on the culprits of paper leak and ensure that no one ever dares to commit this crime."
Article Summary: The National Testing Agency NTA is seeking candidates for four senior positions. The revamp comes amid months of protests over the alleged NEET paper leak. The agency said the initiative was aimed at rebuilding an institution that conducts examinations affecting millions of students every year.

Article Title: 'Agitation does not mean lathicharge': SC on police action against students protesting paper leak
Article Text:
CJI said the Constitution guarantees the right to peaceful protest.

Poll Vote & Share your view Should there be a uniform nationwide protocol for peaceful protests? Strongly agree Disagree 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday said the right to peaceful protest is constitutionally guaranteed and that the mere existence of an agitation cannot justify alleged police excesses against demonstrators.A bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant made the observations while hearing pleas alleging police excesses against students during the July 20 protests over the NEET paper leak.The bench also indicated that a uniform nationwide protocol was needed to facilitate peaceful protests while enabling authorities to act against anti-social elements."Right to peaceful protests is in the Constitution. Right to peaceful protest is absolutely guaranteed. That cannot be denied. Merely because there is agitation cannot justify police excess," the CJI observed.Emphasising the need to protect both protesters and law enforcement personnel, the bench said, "Agitation does not mean lathicharge. Also, agitation does not mean violence."The court said pan-India guidelines should be framed on the issue without either the petitioners or governments adopting an adversarial approach.The bench, however, also expressed concern over allegations of attacks on police personnel during protests.When a lawyer referred to injuries suffered by police personnel and alleged attacks on their families by an unruly mob, Justice Joymalya Bagchi said, "Injury to police is of equal concern. We may call upon the State to respond why adequate safeguards were not provided…"The CJI said there should be a clear protocol governing peaceful protests across the country, including the provision of designated spaces for demonstrations."There should be a protocol when someone wants to agitate peacefully. Proper space for that. There is no impediment in that regard. But if there is any anti-social element that can be dealt with," the CJI said.The court observed that the matter required an all-India approach and indicated that mandatory guidelines could be evolved to ensure uniformity."It’s a question of all India… this uniformity in protocol is also… Self-discipline is integral to the entire process," the CJI observed.The matter has been listed for further hearing on Tuesday.
Article Summary: The Supreme Court said the right to peaceful protest is constitutionally guaranteed. A bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant made the observations while hearing pleas alleging police excesses against students during the NEET paper leak. The bench also indicated that a uniform nationwide protocol was needed to facilitate peaceful protests.

Article Title: 'Former minister will be exposed': Vijay-led Tamil Nadu govt on DMK 'corruption' audit report
Article Text:
Tamil Nadu finance minister N Marie Wilson (PTI file photo)

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu finance minister N Marie Wilson on Sunday said the state government will table an "audit report on corruption" during the upcoming Budget session, alleging that it will expose irregularities in the collection of "party funds" during the previous MK Stalin-led DMK regime.The Vijay-led cabinet's minister made the remarks while addressing an event in Chennai's Harbour Assembly constituency, taking a swipe at the opposition DMK over what he described as attempts to feign ignorance regarding the alleged irregularities. Though he did not name anyone directly, Wilson appeared to target former DMK minister and current Harbour MLA PK Sekar Babu."The former minister who currently represents this constituency now is feigning ignorance about the party funds collected during the DMK rule. He has asked 'what is party funds?' I am constrained to react, since I am addressing my first event in Harbour constituency. We are preparing an audit report on corruption made under the pretext of raising party funds during the previous DMK rule. It will be presented in the upcoming Budget session," Wilson said.In another apparent reference to Sekar Babu, the finance minister added, "It will contain a list of corruption made.Then, this former minister will be exposed."Speaking at the same event, Wilson also reiterated the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) government's commitment to abolishing the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET). He claimed that just as Tamil Nadu witnessed a major political shift in 2026 with the TVK coming to power, a similar change would take place at the national level after the 2029 Lok Sabha elections."There will be a permanent solution for the NEET exam. Our party (TVK) leadership is actively working on a plan to ensure that this exam will be completely abolished. This change will be visible across India," he said while addressing a function organised to distribute commendation certificates to Class 10 and Class 12 students.When asked by reporters to elaborate on the proposed audit report, Wilson declined to share further details, saying, "wait and watch," and indicated that chief minister Vijay would make an announcement on the matter.The first Budget of the Vijay-led TVK government will be presented in the Tamil Nadu assembly on August 5 by Wilson. The assembly's Business Advisory Committee will meet the same day to decide the duration of the Budget session.
Article Summary: Tamil Nadu finance minister N Marie Wilson says state government will table an "audit report on corruption" during the upcoming Budget session. Wilson alleges that it will expose irregularities in the collection of "party funds" during previous MK Stalin-led DMK regime.

Article Title: US FDA nod for 1st pill to replace jabs to fight high cholesterol
Article Text:
Representative image

NEW DELHI: Patients with difficult-to-control high cholesterol could soon have an oral alternative to cholesterol-lowering injections after US Food and Drug Administration approved the world's first oral PCSK9 inhibitor, a class of medicines that dramatically lowers "bad" cholesterol.The tablet, Lipfendra, has been approved for adults with high cholesterol, including those with an inherited condition called heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia.However, the drug is not expected to be available in India immediately. "Even if a medicine is approved abroad, it cannot be marketed in India automatically... it must obtain approval from CDSCO... which may include clinical trials as required under Indian regulations," said Dr Subhash Mandal, national general secretary, Indian Pharmaceutical Association.The approval is significant because many high-risk patients continue to have elevated low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol despite treatment with standard oral medicines.Clinical trials involving 3,207 adults found the once-daily oral drug reduced LDL cholesterol by 56-59% over 24 weeks in patients already on maximally tolerated statins, delivering reductions comparable to injectable PCSK9 inhibitors and offering another option for those whose cholesterol remains uncontrolled despite existing therapy.However, cardiologists said that the drug is unlikely to become a first-line treatment."The new oral therapy lowers LDL... by about 50-60%, making it a promising option for patients who prefer to avoid injections," said Dr Ambuj Roy, Professor of Cardiology at AIIMS Delhi.
Article Summary: Lipfendra is the world's first oral PCSK9 inhibitor, a class of medicines that dramatically lowers "bad" cholesterol. The tablet has been approved for adults with high cholesterol, including those with an inherited condition called heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia. Cardiologists said that the drug is unlikely to become a first-line treatment.

Article Title: India’s first hydrogen-powered train completes over 1,200 km trials, saves 3,200 litres of diesel; onboard fuel cells generate electricity, emit only water vapour
Article Text:
File photo: Jind-Sonipat Hydrogen Train

Train generates electricity using hydrogen fuel cells

Developed indigenously by Indian Railways

Dedicated hydrogen storage facility set up at Jind

Multiple safety systems incorporated

Independent hydrogen leak detection systems

Heat, flame and smoke sensors

Automatic emergency shut-off systems

Continuous ventilation

Compliance with international safety standards

Mandatory technical validations before operations

Delhi trials planned next

India's first hydrogen-powered train has travelled more than 1,200 kilometres since it was flagged off on July 17, with Railways saying the project has already saved over 3,200 litres of diesel during trial operations between Jind and Sonipat in Haryana.According to a railway ministry press release, the successful trial runs have paved the way for the next phase of testing, with operations on the Delhi route expected to begin soon.Prime Minister Narendra Modi flagged off the country's first hydrogen-powered train from Jind under the Centre's Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative.Unlike conventional diesel locomotives, the hydrogen train produces electricity onboard through a chemical reaction between hydrogen and oxygen inside fuel cells, according to the Railway Ministry.The electricity generated powers the train's motors, while water vapour is the only by-product released during the process.Because there is no combustion, the train produces no smoke or tailpipe carbon emissions, making it one of the cleanest forms of rail propulsion currently available, the ministry said.The hydrogen train has been developed as an indigenous project by Indian Railways.According to the railway ministry, the train consists of 10 passenger coaches and two Hydrogen Driving Power Cars that together generate 2,400 kW of power.The propulsion system is supported by lithium iron phosphate batteries along with hydrogen cylinders.Railways minister Ashwini Vaishnaw described the project as a landmark achievement, saying the propulsion system and related technology were developed within India.The project has also led to the establishment of Indian Railways' first dedicated hydrogen storage and refuelling facility at Jind.The railway ministry said green hydrogen is stored at pressures of up to 500 bar and dispensed at 350 bar. The facility has a storage capacity of around 3,000 kilograms of hydrogen to support regular train operations.According to the ministry, the train has been equipped with several safety features, including:The ministry said these measures are intended to ensure the safe operation of hydrogen-powered trains under Indian conditions.Following the successful operations between Jind and Sonipat, Indian Railways plans to begin trial runs on the Delhi route.According to the railway ministry, the project aims to establish an indigenous hydrogen rail ecosystem while supporting the country's transition towards zero-emission rail transport.Officials said the initiative could lay the foundation for wider deployment of hydrogen-powered trains across India in the future.
Article Summary: India's first hydrogen-powered train has travelled more than 1,200 kilometres since it was flagged off on July 17. The project has already saved over 3,200 litres of diesel during trial operations between Jind and Sonipat in Haryana. Indian Railways plans to begin trial runs on the Delhi route soon.

Article Title: CJP's win fuels call by 'E20 Janta Party' for no-ethanol option
Article Text:
Delhi Taxi and Tourist Transporters and Tour Operators Association have announced a march to Parliament against E20 petrol on Aug 4

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think consumers should have the option to buy 100% petrol? Yes, consumers should have a choice No, the current policy is enough 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Inspired by Cockroach Janta Party's campaign over the NEET paper leak that led to Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation as education minister, a new outfit - E20 Janta Party - has stepped into the ring, demanding consumers be given the option of buying 100% petrol and seeking the resignation of road transport and highways minister Nitin Gadkari.The campaign has found support among transporters, with Delhi Taxi and Tourist Transporters and Tour Operators Association announcing a march to Parliament against E20 petrol on August 4.The association alleged that the ethanol-blending policy has reduced fuel efficiency, increased maintenance costs and affected engine performance, particularly in older vehicles.Also Read: Ethanol blended fuel damaged vehicles of people, claims Maharashtra Congress chief E20 Janta Party, which gained more than 25,000 followers on X in a few hours Sunday, said it was not seeking subsidies, free fuel or withdrawal of ethanol-blended petrol, but only demanding that consumers be given the choice to buy the fuel they want.It also demanded transparent fuel labelling so consumers knew what they were buying, publication of data on the costs, benefits and impact of fuel blends, and independent studies on mileage, engine performance, emissions and maintenance costs.Although ethanol-free 100-octane premium petrol has long been available in the country, it is sold only at select fuel stations and costs Rs 169 per litre, compared with Rs 102.12 per litre for standard E20 fuel (in Delhi).Minister of state for petroleum Suresh Gopi told Parliament last week that govt had not received "widespread or substantiated" complaints on ethanol-blended petrol affecting vehicle performance.
Article Summary: E20 Janta Party has stepped into the ring, demanding consumers be given the option of buying 100% petrol. The campaign has found support among transporters, with Delhi Taxi and Tourist Transporters and Tour Operators Association announcing a march to Parliament.

Article Title: At no point did government stop students from protesting: Nirmala Sitharaman
Article Text:
File photo: Union finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman

NEW DELHI: Government did not stop students from protesting at any point in time, while at the same time, it was gearing up to conduct the NEET re-examination in time and punish the culprits who had engaged in paper leaks, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said."Permission was given when they came, as soon as Dipke landed. We didn't try at any point in time to stop the protest at all. When things didn't go right at the first time when the exams were held and leak became public, and it had to be acted upon, soon the govt arrested those who had bought and sold the papers. It was the responsibility of the govt to arrest them and put into the judicial process... but equally important was that the re-examination happens in time, so that one whole year does not get affected," Sitharaman said on why the govt took long to respond to the students' protest.She stressed it was after the successful re-examination that education minister Dharmendra Pradhan took the "wise" decision to resign. "If he hadn't done that (the re-examination process), it would have been irresponsible of everybody in the system," she said.Besides, she said, India faced the risk of inflation from both external and internal factors. "...this year, there is El Nino. The catchment areas are not receiving adequate rains. So, water for irrigation and drinking is going to pose a challenge. So, inflation cannot be just imported. It is also our own," she said.
Article Summary: Government did not stop students from protesting at any point in time, says Nirmala Sitharaman. At the same time, it was gearing up to conduct the NEET re- examination in time and punish the culprits who had engaged in paper leaks.

Article Title: India saw more than 5,000 child adoptions last year, highest in a decade
Article Text:
Representative image

392 special needs kids adopted last year, increase of 25% over 2024-25

NEW DELHI: Amid challenges ranging from nearly 26,000 people waiting to adopt kids to only a limited number of children available in the most-sought-after 0-2 age group with adoption agencies, as many as 5,022 children were adopted between April 2025 and March 2026 - the highest in over a decade - as per data shared by Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) since 2015-16.According to CARA, as many as 4,603 children were adopted domestically and inter-country adoptions accounted for 419 children.The number of children adopted in 2024-25 stood at 4,515. Of all the children who are declared free for adoption and available in the adoption pool of Specialised Adoption Agencies (SAAs) across India, 80% are in the special needs category.In 2015-16, according to the CARA data, the total figure stood at 3,677, and breached the 4,000 mark in 2018-19 for the first time. It fell during the pandemic, before rising again in 2023-24 to cross 4,000 again.While very young children who come into the pool are immediately adopted by prospective adoptive parents (PAPs), the number of older and special needs children keeps adding up as they remain in the pool. The average waiting time for adoption is estimated to be about three years for infants and young children.Amid these challenges, CARA CEO Bhavna Saxena attributes the increase in adoptions to a focused strategy on following up with specialised adoption agencies and child welfare committees through CARA’s ‘identification cell’ to ensure that eligible children in the institutions are declared free for adoption without delays.According to the CARA database, of the 5,022 adoptions, 2,756 were of girls, 2,263 of boys and three were in the ‘others’ category. According to officials, the adoption of girls saw an increase of 8% over 2024-25 when 2,554 girls were adopted. That more girls figure on the adoption list compared to boys is in keeping with past trends.Officials point out that while many more prospective parents opting for the girl child reflects a change in mindset, there is also a view among organisations working on adoptions that the higher numbers have to do with the fact that more girls end up in adoption agencies and orphanages and are, therefore, available in the adoption pool.According to the CARA CEO, there is greater focus now on building awareness about special needs children so that parents who appear keen can be counselled and assisted to go for a special needs child.“We started the process of holding regional consultations last year and found that parents were getting encouraged to consider children with special needs. We will be strengthening the outreach this year,” Saxena further added.She said 392 special needs children were adopted last year, marking an increase of around 25% over 2024-25, when the number was 313. Also, adoptions by relatives and step-parents went up by 50%, from 820 to 1,231.Saxena said that to strengthen the system, 118 new child welfare committees were constituted and 52 new specialised agencies registered over past one year. As many as 266 new SAAs have been registered and activated since July 2024.
Article Summary: As many as 5,022 children were adopted between April 2025 and March 2026. 392 special needs kids adopted last year, increase of 25% over 2024-25. Of all the children who are declared free for adoption and available in the adoption pool of Specialised Adoption Agencies, 80% are in the special needs category.

Article Title: Nepal seeks India's approval for biometric national identity card as travel document
Article Text:
Nepal seeks India's approval for biometric National Identity card as travel document (ANI image)

Nepal plans to replace citizenship certificates

India reviews the proposal

The Kathmandu Post

Nepal has formally requested India's approval to recognise its biometric National Identity (NID) card as an official travel document for cross-border journeys, alongside passports and citizenship certificates.At present, Nepali citizens travelling to India, particularly by air, must carry either a valid passport or an original citizenship certificate. Indian citizens entering Nepal are required to present either a passport or an original voter identity card with a photograph.However, Nepal's National Identity card contains biometric information, including fingerprints, facial images and iris scans. The programme was launched as a pilot in Panchthar district and among government employees in 2009. So far, more than 4.5 million Nepali citizens have received the card, while nearly 20 million applications have been submitted.The request comes as Nepal gradually makes the biometric National Identity card mandatory for banking, land registration, passport issuance and access to public services, with plans to eventually replace citizenship certificates."In the long run, we will have a single identity card replacing the citizenship certificate.It is verified, authentic and technology-friendly," Tiwari said."That is why we have requested India to allow the use of the National Identity Card while travelling by both air and land routes," he added.According to senior immigration officials quoted by, an Indian Embassy delegation met officials from Nepal's Department of Immigration earlier this week to discuss the proposalThe delegation was reportedly "positive" about the initiative and informed Nepalese officials that the request had been forwarded to authorities in New Delhi for consideration."We have already forwarded the proposal to the Indian side through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs," said Ram Chandra Tiwari, Director General of the Department of Immigration.Officials from Nepal's Home Ministry also said that discussions have included creating formal mechanisms to record cross-border travel data and better manage movement between the two neighbouring countries.
Article Summary: Nepal has formally requested India's approval to recognise its biometric National Identity (NID) card as an official travel document. At present, Nepali citizens travelling to India, particularly by air, must carry either a valid passport or original citizenship certificate. Indian citizens entering Nepal are required to present either a passport or an original voter identity card with a photograph.

Article Title: 3 Indians die in workplace accidents in Gulf every week, shows MEA data
Article Text:
Most Indians in the Gulf are employed in sectors like construction, retail, warehouses and automobiles, where occupational risks are high.

Further, to ensure women’s safety, only state-run agencies have been authorised to recruit female workers holding ECR passports to the Gulf through the e-Migrate portal, the minister said.

HYDERABAD: Over 800 Indian expats died in workplace accidents between 2023 and 2025, according to MEA data. Of these, 55% occurred in Gulf countries, which recorded nearly three deaths a week on an average. The latest incident — the Qatar blast that killed 12 Indians last month — has renewed calls for scrutiny of safety lapses.According to MEA data, Saudi Arabia recorded the highest toll, with 182 deaths over the three-year period — more than one Indian worker every week — followed by UAE with 128 fatalities.A majority of suicides during the period were also reported from Gulf nations, underscoring the challenges faced by migrant workers.Telangana NRI Migrants’ Association attributed the recurring fatalities to multiple factors: inadequate use of safety equipment, poor adherence to workplace safety protocols, technical failures at industrial sites and insufficient skill and safety training.Many workers, they said, labour in temperatures exceeding 45 degrees Celsius and return to accommodations cooled to 20 degrees Celsius, exposing their bodies to temperature swings of 20-25 degrees Celsius, which can lead to serious health complications.Most Indians in the Gulf are employed in sectors like construction, retail, warehouses and automobiles, where occupational risks are high.“At times, workers neglect their own safety by failing to wear protective gear such as helmets, boots and gloves while working in hazardous industries. In several cases, they are unaware of the risks,” said Manda Bheem Reddy, vice-chairman, Telangana NRI Cell.The high number of suicides, the migrants’ welfare association said, is often driven by cramped quarters and poor-quality food, coupled with extremely hectic work schedules. “Also, workers often go without salaries for up to three months while putting in shifts of 12 hours a day. Even when wages are paid, deductions are common, adding to their str-ess,” said B M Vinod Kumar, chairman, Telangana govt’s NRI advisory committee.Many employers allegedly evade responsibility by attributing workplace deaths to “natural causes” such as heart attacks, Vinod claimed. Only a few provide compensation through insurance coverage.According to MEA, govt accords high priority to the safety and well-being of Indians abroad and there are channels to enable them to reach out to missions.Kirti Vardhan Singh, minister of state for external affairs, said in Rajya Sabha that Pravasi Bharatiya Sahayata Kendras have been set up in locations such as New Delhi, Dubai, Riyadh and Jeddah. “There are dedicated labour wings... Indian missions regularly organise open house and consular camps in remote areas to get feedback from the workers...,” she said.Further, to ensure women’s safety, only state-run agencies have been authorised to recruit female workers holding ECR passports to the Gulf through the e-Migrate portal, the minister said.
Article Summary: Over 800 Indian expats died in workplace accidents between 2023 and 2025, according to MEA data. Of these, 55% occurred in Gulf countries, which recorded nearly three deaths a week on an average. Most Indians in the Gulf are employed in sectors like construction, retail, warehouses and automobiles.

Article Title: ‘Banned chemical’: CPCB red-flags new ‘green’ crackers
Article Text:
The Centre had asked CSIR-NEERI to develop green/low-emission fireworks with pollution reduction of more than 50% in association with fireworks manufacturers

NEW DELHI: There is no unanimity on allowing commercial production of next-generation green firecrackers in the country, with two govt organisations taking contradictory stands in Supreme Court Council of Scientific and Industrial Research - National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-NEERI) has approved the new formulations, stating that they reduce pollution levels by 40-60%. In contrast, Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has objected, arguing that these crackers still contain barium nitrate - a chemical banned by the SC - and, therefore, cannot be permitted.The Centre had asked CSIR-NEERI to develop green/low-emission fireworks with pollution reduction of more than 50% in association with fireworks manufacturers. Thereafter, Tamil Nadu Fireworks and Amorces Manufacturers' Association (TANFAMA) devised new-generation fireworks formulations with reduced quantity of barium salts/nitrates in combination with other oxidisers for particulate emission reduction of more than 50%.As per the CSIR-NEERI report, emission reductions achieved for PM10 and PM2.5 were between 45% and 60%, and recommended that these formulations for light-emission fireworks, such as flowerpots, sparklers, chakkars, pencils and twinkling stars and their hybrids, may be considered for commercial production.It also approved manufacture of joined crackers, known as 'ladis', which have been banned as per the court's order. The report said there was a reduction in particulate matter (PM) emissions by approximately 30% and a reduction in solid waste generation by up to 32% for joined crackers.Responding to the CSIR-NEERI report, CPCB raised objection on how barium nitrate could be used in crackers as it was banned by the apex court and allowing their production would be in violation of the court's order. "This court, vide order dated Oct 23, 2018, has expressly banned the use of barium salts in firecrackers and, therefore, any formulation involving barium compounds, even in reduced quantities, is in contravention of the said order," the board said."The reported reduction in PM10 and PM2.5 levels has not been comparatively assessed with (i) improved low-emission crackers and (ii) green crackers formulated entirely without barium, rendering the claim incomplete and inconclusive," it further said.Caught between contradictory stands taken by two expert bodies, the ministry of environment, forest and climate change filed an affidavit bringing it to the apex court's notice and left it to the SC to take a decision on the issue. It also informed the court that the composition of new-generation firecrackers was sent to the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO), which is the regulatory body for explosive substances, and it had given a no-objection certificate to the new formulation of firecrackers.
Article Summary: There is no unanimity on allowing commercial production of next-generation green firecrackers. Supreme Court Council of Scientific and Industrial Research - National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-NEERI) has approved the new formulations. Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has objected, arguing that these crackers still contain barium nitrate.

Article Title: 'No responsibilities': Mohan Bhagwat on live-in relationships; says marriage 'instils dharma'
Article Text:
RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat (File photo)

NEW DELHI: Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat on Sunday described marriage as a discipline that "instils dharma", while saying that the "reality of live-in relationships can be seen all over the world.""Marriage is a discipline which instils dharma. Its alternative is live-in relationship. Modernity. What are its consequences? We don't want responsibilities but happiness. Stay together when it is wanted and part ways when not wanted. No responsibilities. What will grow with it? What is growing, look around the world," PTI quoted Bhagwat as saying.The RSS chief was addressing an event in Hyderabad.He, however, stressed that modernity was also necessary and that adapting to changing times was "part of the country's traditions."In an apparent reference to live-in relationships, Bhagwat described them as a "degradation" and "blind imitation of Western culture", while welcoming modernity.He also maintained that LGBTQ people are a part of society and should not be looked down upon.Bhagwat favoured parents following mobile phone discipline and stressed the importance of conversations among family members to address the questions of the younger generation and various family-related issues.Addressing concerns over the lifestyle choices of the younger generation, including excessive mobile phone use, he urged elders to practise what they want to see in their children."Be the change you want to see in society. Reduce your time on social media. Follow mobile discipline. We look to the government. In our tradition, the government is second; society is first. (We say) the government should make this law or that law... we can do that at our home," he said."We tell children about mobile discipline, but we are attached to mobiles. So much so that a mother gives a mobile to a child if the child is crying," Bhagwat added.He further argued that British rule made Indians believe that everything ancient was "worthless," adding that Western countries were facing problems due to an incomplete vision of various issues that India had also adopted.
Article Summary: Mohan Bhagwat: Marriage is a discipline which instils dharma. Its alternative is live-in relationship. Modernity. What are its consequences? We don't want responsibilities but happiness. Stay together when it is wanted and part ways when not wanted.

Article Title: 'Attempt to repair PM's tarnished image': Congress on high-powered exam reforms task force
Article Text:
PM Narendra Modi; Jairam Ramesh

NEW DELHI: Reacting to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's announcement of a high-powered task force on examination reforms, the Congress on Sunday termed it a "high-powered attempt" by the prime minister to "repair" his "irreparably tarnished image. ""Friends, in June 2024, after irregularities in several exams, including NEET-UG, the Modi government formed a high-level expert committee chaired by former ISRO chairman Dr K. Radhakrishnan to 'ensure the transparent, smooth, and fair conduct of examinations.' In July 2026, after irregularities once again in NEET-UG and other exams, the Modi government has formed a 'high-level task force' to focus on exam reforms," Congress MP Jairam Ramesh wrote on X shortly after Prime Minister Narendra Modi's announcement.He added that the government was yet to fully implement the 101 recommendations made by the Radhakrishnan committee."Instead, for nearly two years between 2024 and 2026, it did not even appoint a full-time director general for the National Testing Agency (NTA). Ultimately, all of this is nothing but a high-powered attempt to repair the Prime Minister's irreparably tarnished image," Ramesh said.PM Modi's announcement came amid demands for examination reforms following the NEET (UG) question paper leak controversy, which affected over 22 lakh aspirants.On Saturday, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online satirical platform, ended its indefinite sit-in at Delhi's Jantar Mantar, demanding the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan and broader education reforms.CJP ended its agitation hours after Pradhan resigned, as student protests intensified in Delhi and other parts of the country. Union Minister Pralhad Joshi has been given additional charge of the Ministry of Education.Meanwhile, besides Nilekani, who co-founded IT giant Infosys, other members of the high-powered task force include former Isro chairman S Somanath, ex-Intelligence Bureau director Tapan Deka, IIT Madras director V Kamakoti, former education secretary Anita Karwal, and logistics expert Amrit Lal Meena.According to the prime minister, the government will implement the task force's recommendations to establish a "foolproof examination system."The panel will help revamp NTA examinations, with a focus on technology-driven improvements and structural reforms in the system, PM Modi added.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a high-powered task force on examination reforms. Congress MP Jairam Ramesh called it a "high-powered attempt" by the prime minister to "repair" his "irreparably tarnished image" PM Modi's announcement came amid demands for examination reforms following the NEET (UG) question paper leak controversy.

Article Title: CDSCO cancels 7 clinical trial ethics panels over serious violations
Article Text: NEW DELHI: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has cancelled the registration of seven Ethics Committees across India overseeing clinical trials after inspections found serious violations of regulatory norms. The regulator said the committees failed to comply with the New Drugs and Clinical Trials (NDCT) Rules, 2019, Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guidelines and other requirements, compromising their ability to carry out their responsibilities.The action covers Ethics Committees in Delhi, Pune, Navi Mumbai, Ahmedabad and Kolkata, which review and monitor clinical trials to protect the rights, safety and well-being of participants.The CDSCO said the committees were inspected as part of a risk-based compliance exercise to assess adherence to the NDCT Rules, 2019, Good Clinical Practice guidelines and quality management systems. The inspections identified significant deficiencies and major regulatory non-compliances in the functioning of the committees.According to the regulator, the registrations were cancelled only after completion of the regulatory process, including evaluation of inspection reports, review of Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) responses, issuance of show-cause notices and personal hearings, wherever applicable.The seven committees whose registrations have been cancelled are Rational Independent Ethics Committee, New Delhi; Hurip Independent Bioethics Committee and Dr T K Pal Memorial Bio Ethics Committee, Kolkata; Ethiwell Ethics Committee and Ethos Ethics Committee, Navi Mumbai; Institutional Ethics Committee, Aatman Hospital, Ahmedabad; and Royal Pune Independent Ethics Committee, Pune.
Article Summary: The action covers Ethics Committees in Delhi, Pune, Navi Mumbai, Ahmedabad and Kolkata. The committees review and monitor clinical trials to protect the rights, safety and well-being of participants. The CDSCO said the committees were inspected as part of a risk-based compliance exercise.

Article Title: Infosys co-founder, Aadhaar architect: Who is Nandan Nilekani, set to lead high-powered exam reforms task force

NEW DELHI: Continuing his announcements on examination reforms, Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday said the government has constituted a high-powered task force to be led by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani "HIGH-POWERED TASK FORCE on examination reforms under the leadership of Shri Nandan Nilekani constituted," PM Modi said in a video message on X, a day after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a satirical platform, called off its 37-day-long agitation following the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the alleged NEET (UG) question paper leak.Led by CJP, thousands of students had been on an indefinite sit-in in Delhi since June 21, demanding the resignation or removal of Pradhan and broader reforms in the education sector.Meanwhile, joining Nilekani on the task force are former Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro) chairman S Somanath, former Intelligence Bureau (IB) director Tapan Deka, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras director V Kamakoti, former education secretary Anita Karwal, and logistics expert Amrit Lal Meena.Nilekani is the co-founder and chairman of Bengaluru-headquartered IT giant Infosys. Article Title: Beyond Tigers: The wildlife trade fuelled by pets and myths
Article Text:
Binturong

Coolie

From forest animal to social-media prop

Egyptian vulture

When beauty and belief become threats

A crisis hiding in plain sight

The bazaar and the smartphone

Shikra

Looking beyond the flagship species

Dr. Ridhima Solanki holds a PhD in Natural Resources and Wildlife Sciences and a Master's in Forestry, with over a decade of experience shaping wildlife policy and practice across India and Southeast Asia.

Somewhere in the collective memory of Indian cinema perches Allah Rakha, the trained bird of prey fromthat generations of filmgoers grew up watching. It was a small but glamorous detail in a blockbuster, a wild creature transformed into a loyal companion. It would be difficult to prove that any one film encouraged the wildlife trade. Yet such portrayals can make proximity to a wild animal appear exciting, harmless and even aspirational. The reality behind that image is far less charming.A 2020 study of Facebook groups and pages in Thailand recorded 396 raptors and owls offered for sale between February 2015 and June 2019. These included nine shikras. Researchers found evidence that wild birds, including chicks taken from nests, were being offered online; one juvenile shikra was explicitly advertised as wild-caught.The falcon story, then, is not an isolated cultural memory. It points to a trade that has moved from cages in traditional markets to photographs, private messages and social-media listings.Earlier this month, a joint operation by the Central Bureau of Investigation and the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence, supported by the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau, recovered 53 protected animals and birds from locations in Maharashtra and West Bengal.The haul included 15 slow lorises, two binturongs, 28 star tortoises, six Egyptian vultures and two shikras. Six people were arrested in connection with what investigators described as an alleged interstate wildlife-trafficking syndicate. The investigation remains under way. The raid was an important enforcement success. It was also a window into a conservation crisis that rarely receives the attention reserved for tiger skins, elephant ivory or rhino horn.Slow lorises are especially vulnerable to the visual economy of the exotic-pet trade. Their large eyes and seemingly gentle movements make them attractive subjects for videos, tourist photographs and online posts. What looks endearing on a screen can conceal capture, transport, injury and prolonged stress.Studies of the tourist-photo trade have documented nocturnal slow lorises being exposed to bright lights and repeated flash photography, conditions that can disrupt their natural activity patterns and potentially damage their light-sensitive eyes.The physical toll can be severe. Researchers examining 77 confiscated greater slow lorises taken to a rehabilitation centre in Indonesia found that 28.6% died within six months, mostly because of traumatic injuries. All the infants in the group died. External wounds, dental problems and abnormal behaviour were common among those that survived. The study did not claim that every injury occurred during capture or transport, but it demonstrated the extraordinary welfare cost carried by animals moving through the illegal trade.By the time a wild animal appears in someone’s home or on a tourist’s shoulder, others may already have died along the supply chain. The binturong faces a similar pressure. A 2024 study of online trade in Indonesia found 594 advertisements offering 724 live binturongs, with 97.6% of the listings appearing on Facebook. Researchers concluded that the exotic-pet trade appeared to be the principal source of demand in their dataset. Although the exact origins of most animals could not be established, the authors argued that a large share were probably taken illegally from the wild. Seizure records from 2015 to 2023 included 103 live binturongs. The evidence comes from Indonesia, and should not automatically be treated as a measure of the trade in India. But it shows how quickly demand for a relatively little-known forest animal can grow once buyers and sellers find one another online.Not every trafficked animal is bought for the same reason. The Indian star tortoise is prized for the striking pattern on its shell and is widely sought in the exotic-pet trade. In some markets, demand is also reinforced by beliefs that tortoises bring luck, prosperity or blessings. Those beliefs may sound benign, but they can turn a wild animal into an object of possession and encourage the removal of thousands of individuals from their natural habitat.The Egyptian vultures recovered during the CBI-DRI operation require more careful interpretation. The official release confirms their recovery but does not say why they were being traded or what the intended buyers planned to do with them. It would therefore be premature to attribute this particular seizure to occult practices, medicine or any other specific purpose. What is clear is that the Egyptian vulture is already endangered and faces several established threats, including poisoning, unsafe veterinary drugs, electrocution and the ingestion of contaminated carcasses. Illegal capture or trade adds another hazard to a species that has little room left for additional pressure.The larger lesson is that wildlife trafficking is not one market. It is a collection of overlapping markets driven by pets, status, food, traditional practices, decorative value and beliefs about luck or healing. Different species enter the chain for different reasons, but the result is often the same, an animal is removed from the wild and reduced to a commodity.Public attention to wildlife crime naturally gravitates towards tigers, elephants and rhinos. Sustained focus on these species has helped strengthen legislation, enforcement and public awareness. But the success of flagship-species conservation can create a blind spot. It can leave the impression that the broader war on wildlife trafficking is being won, even as birds, reptiles, primates and small carnivores continue to move through less visible networks.A Lok Sabha reply issued in August 2025 listed 820 wildlife-crime cases reported to the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau in 2020, followed by 632 in 2021, 546 in 2022, 349 in 2023 and 354 in 2024. These were cases registered and reported by state and central enforcement agencies. They are not estimates of the total number of wildlife crimes committed.The numbers therefore require care. The broad decline may indicate better deterrence, changing enforcement priorities or variations in reporting. It may also reflect the growing difficulty of detecting transactions that have moved online. The small increase from 349 cases in 2023 to 354 in 2024 also means the series is not an uninterrupted annual fall. A detected case tells us that enforcement found something. A falling number of detected cases does not, by itself, tell us whether the underlying trade is shrinking.The modern wildlife trade does not require the dark web. Ordinary social-media platforms are sufficient. A photograph can function as a shop window. The price can be negotiated through a private message. Buyers and sellers may never meet until the animal is delivered or handed to an intermediary. Research on the online trade in raptors and binturongs shows how public or semi-private social-media groups can connect sellers with a large customer base while making monitoring difficult.But the smartphone has not replaced the traditional wildlife market. The two systems can coexist. Repeated enforcement operations at Delhi’s Kabutar Market near Jama Masjid illustrate the resilience of the physical trade. Wildlife SOS reported that 1,741 birds, including around 500 chicks, were recovered in a 2022 operation. In July 2024, the Delhi Forest Department recovered around 1,000 birds following a complaint by PETA India. Nearly 150 more parakeets and pigeons were recovered in another operation that December.These figures do not establish that every trader in the market is involved in illegal activity. They do, however, show that protected native birds have repeatedly been found within an established commercial space. An IndiaSpend investigation into bird markets in Delhi, Patna and Lucknow also reported sales of protected species, poor welfare conditions and widespread non-compliance with registration requirements. Such findings should be attributed to the specific investigation rather than used to condemn every pet-shop owner or vendor in those cities.Under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Pet Shop) Rules, establishments selling live animals are required to register and maintain prescribed welfare and record-keeping standards. Separately, the Wild Life (Protection) Act regulates the possession and trade of protected wildlife. Registration as a pet shop does not authorise a business to sell a protected native species.Raids matter. They rescue individual animals, disrupt supply chains and create consequences for traffickers. But repeated recoveries from the same markets show the limits of enforcement that addresses supply without reducing demand. Protecting biodiversity will require closer monitoring of online platforms, better coordination among forest departments, police, customs authorities and courier networks, and consistent action against the illegal sale of protected species. Social-media companies must also become more effective at identifying and removing wildlife-sale posts rather than relying largely on outside researchers and activists to flag them.Public behaviour matters just as much. A person posing with a nocturnal primate may see only an unusual holiday photograph. A buyer taking home a tortoise may believe that one small purchase cannot harm a species. Someone sharing an exotic-pet video may not know whether the animal was legally bred or pulled from the wild.But demand is built from individual acts. Every impulsive purchase, paid photograph and viral post can add value to the next animal waiting to be captured. South Asia’s conservation story cannot end with the tiger, the elephant or the rhino. Its future also depends on the shikra in the cage, the loris under the camera flash, the tortoise hidden inside a bag and the binturong advertised through a phone screen. These are the creatures that rarely command front pages. They are also the ones the wildlife trade is counting on nobody to notice.
Article Summary: The exotic-pet trade has moved from cages in traditional markets to photographs, private messages and social-media listings. A 2020 study of Facebook groups and pages in Thailand recorded 396 raptors and owls offered for sale between February 2015 and June 2019. Six people were arrested in connection with what investigators described as an alleged interstate wildlife-trafficking syndicate.

NEW DELHI: With the nationwide cumulative monsoon rainfall deficit hovering at more than 15% despite good rains in certain parts, Prime Minister Narendra Modi , in his monthly radio programme 'Man Ki Baat ' on Sunday, flagged the importance of water conservation measures through the 'catch the rain’ campaign and appealed to people to take responsibility for a pond, well or step-well in their vicinity and save every drop of water.Aim of the 'catch the rain' campaign, that has been underway since July 4, is to conserve the water right where and when the rain falls.“Under this initiative, fresh momentum is being given to rainwater harvesting, groundwater recharge, the rejuvenation of old water bodies and tree plantation. Article Title: Can the government take control of foreign-funded assets? FCRA Bill explained
Article Text:
India first enacted the FCRA in 1976 during the Emergency era.

The FCRA Bill treats minorities as enemies and is keen on snatching their properties. DMK MP P Wilson

What is FCRA

FCRA... ensures that foreign money enters India through a registered, accountable and disclosed channel... while enabling thousands of organisations to carry out legitimate, impactful work Centre

FCRA restricts foreign funding that may threaten India's sovereignty.

A law that has steadily become stricter

How FCRA steadily become stricter

What the 2026 Bill proposes

FCRA regulates foreign funding that may threaten national interest.

Why the controversy?



FCRA can be used in 9 different sectors

Government sees law as consistent with global trends.

Why Christian organisations are worried

FRCRA like rules in different countries.

Congress echos similar concerns



FCRA myths

The government's response

Govt's clarification on FCRA

In India, the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA) is one of those laws that returns to the spotlight every few years — often amid much clamour. But why? The law has repeatedly generated debate over how India should balance scrutiny of overseas funding with the autonomy of NGOs and other civil society organisations.The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, introduced in the Lok Sabha in March, proposes a new framework for managing foreign contributions and assets when an organisation’s registration is cancelled, surrendered or ceases. The government says the changes are intended to address administrative and legal gaps, while critics question the breadth of the proposed powers.The opposition, however, has argued that the proposed changes hand sweeping powers to the government and could allow it to take control of assets built over decades by charitable organisations.Several church groups, particularly in the Northeast, have argued that the changes could disproportionately affect Christian institutions that use foreign donations for welfare work.So, what exactly is changing, why has the Bill become controversial and what does it mean for thousands of organisations that receive money from abroad?The Foreign Contribution Regulation Act, popularly known as FCRA, governs how individuals, trusts, NGOs, associations and companies in India can receive and use money, securities or other contributions from foreign sources.Administered by the Amit Shah-led home ministry, the law does not prohibit foreign donations. Instead, it lays down who can receive them, how they must be accounted for and where they can be spent.The government has maintained that the purpose behind the tweaking of the legislation is to ensure foreign money enters India through a more transparent and accountable system so that it cannot be diverted towards activities considered “harmful” to national interest, democratic institutions or public order.Under the law, any organisation that wants to receive regular foreign funding must obtain an FCRA registration from the home ministry. For those receiving a one-time grant for a specific purpose can seek prior permission instead.Therefore, every rupee received has to pass through a designated bank account, be audited and be reported annually to the government.The law also bars election candidates, legislators, judges, government servants, newspaper editors involved in news reporting and political parties from receiving foreign contributions altogether.The government argues that this is not unique to India. The home ministry has cited foreign-influence registration systems in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and Canada to argue that such oversight is not unique to India. However, these systems differ in scope and are not direct equivalents of the FCRA’s broader regulation of foreign contributions.India first enacted the FCRA in 1976 during the Emergency era. Even then, the central concern was “foreign influence” over domestic politics and institutions.The framework was significantly overhauled in 2010, when Parliament replaced the old law with the present FCRA. One of the biggest changes was introducing a registration system valid for five years, after which organisations had to renew their licences.In 2020, the law underwent one of its most significant revisions, mandating the organisations receiving foreign funds to route all contributions through a single State Bank of India branch in New Delhi.The ceiling on administrative expenses was reduced from 50 per cent to 20 per cent. Organisations were also barred from transferring foreign funds to other NGOs, while office-bearers had to provide Aadhaar or passport details.Successive amendments have tightened both reporting requirements and operational restrictions. The 2026 Bill extends the framework beyond routine compliance to the management and disposal of assets when an organisation’s registration ends.The headline provision in the Bill concerns organisations whose FCRA registration comes to an end.At present, an organisation may lose its FCRA registration if the government cancels it for violating the law, if the organisation voluntarily surrenders it or if the registration is not renewed.The 2026 Bill formally introduces the concept of a certificate "ceasing" to exist. This would happen if an organisation fails to apply for renewal, misses the renewal deadline or if its renewal application is rejected.That change is significant because the Bill links the end of an FCRA certificate with what happens to foreign-funded assets.The proposed law creates a designated authority to take charge of foreign contributions and assets created using those contributions whenever an organisation's registration is cancelled, surrendered or ceases.Initially, the transfer of assets will be provisional. If the organisation later succeeds in restoring or renewing its registration, the unutilised foreign contributions and assets will be returned.However, if the organisation fails to regain its registration within the prescribed period, the transfer becomes permanent.The designated authority will then have the power to manage those assets, transfer them to central or state government departments or dispose of them through sale. The proceeds from such disposal, along with any remaining foreign contribution, will be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.The Bill also formally defines "key functionaries" who can be held responsible for violations committed by an organisation. These include directors, trustees, partners, office-bearers and others responsible for managing the institution.It requires organisations receiving foreign funds through prior permission to receive and utilise those funds within a prescribed period.Interestingly, the Bill reduces the maximum punishment for violating the Act from five years' imprisonment to one year, a move the government describes as a more proportionate approach to enforcement.Another provision says no investigation into an offence under the Act may be initiated without the prior approval of the central government. The ministry says this would prevent multiple investigations under a central law; the Bill does not specify the criteria or timeframe for granting such approval.As of July 15, 2026, the FCRA portal listed 22,498 cancelled registrations, 15,212 expired registrations and 14,449 active certificates, according to PRS Legislative Research. The government says the lack of a detailed mechanism for handling assets after registration ends has created administrative uncertainty.The government says the designated authority would fill this procedural gap and ensure that permanently vested assets are used for public purposes. Yet it is precisely this argument that has become the biggest point of disagreement.Critics contest that the Bill goes beyond administrative housekeeping and fundamentally changes the relationship between the government and organisations that receive foreign donations. They argue that the proposed provisions could permanently deprive charities of assets they created over decades, even in situations where they no longer depend on foreign funding. That disagreement lies at the heart of the political and religious controversy surrounding the Bill.The central dispute is whether assets created in the past with foreign contributions should vest in the ‘designated authority’ when an organisation no longer has an active FCRA certificate.That is where the government's reasoning and the opposition's objections diverge. Under the proposed law, assets created using foreign contributions will vest in the “designated authority” not only when an organisation's registration is cancelled or surrendered but also when it simply ceases because the registration was not renewed or the renewal application was rejected.The government argues this merely formalises an existing principle. It points out that the 2010 Act already provided for vesting of foreign-funded assets when an FCRA registration was cancelled or surrendered.According to the ministry of home affairs, the amendment only creates a detailed statutory framework explaining how those assets should be supervised, managed and disposed of, something that the earlier law did not spell out. It also says the initial vesting will be provisional and assets will be returned if the organisation later restores its registration.Critics, however, believe the practical consequences are far more significant. They argue that an organisation may have built a hospital, school or library years ago with foreign donations but may now be running it entirely through domestic funding. If such an organisation decides not to renew its FCRA registration because it no longer needs foreign contributions, the Bill could still result in those earlier assets vesting with the designated authority.PRS Legislative Research illustrates this concern through a hypothetical example of a healthcare organisation that built a hospital using foreign donations but later operated it entirely with domestic funds. Under the proposed framework, the hospital could still vest in the “designated authority” if the organisation's registration ceased and was not restored. The authority would then have the power to transfer it to a government department or dispose of it.Critics therefore argue that the amendment effectively creates no practical exit route from the FCRA system. An organisation wishing to retain assets originally built with foreign contributions may feel compelled to continue renewing its registration indefinitely, even if it no longer receives foreign funding. Another concern relates to mixed funding.The Bill says assets created wholly or partly through foreign contributions can vest in the designated authority. In cases where domestic and foreign funds have both been used to build an asset, organisations may apply to recover the identifiable domestic portion. Critics say that, in practice, separating domestic and foreign contributions within a single building or facility may not always be possible.While the existing law provides a mechanism to appeal against cancellation of an FCRA certificate, critics note that neither the Act nor the proposed amendment specifically provides an appeal against refusal to renew a certificate before the assets vest. They also point out that organisations are not guaranteed an opportunity to be heard before renewal is denied.Although the Bill applies uniformly to all organisations, much of the opposition has come from church groups, especially in the Northeast.The Bill is not religion-specific, but church groups, particularly in Mizoram, have been among its most vocal opponents because many affiliated institutions receive foreign donations for welfare projects.Many churches and Christian charitable institutions receive foreign donations to run schools, hospitals, orphanages, homes for persons with disabilities and other welfare projects. Leaders fear that if their FCRA registrations lapse or renewal is denied, properties developed over decades using foreign contributions could eventually pass into government control. These concerns have been particularly strong in Mizoram.Chief minister Lalduhoma held consultations with leaders of the Council of Churches Mizoram and the Mizoram Kohhran Hruaitute Committee, after which it was decided that the provisions of the Bill "cannot be accepted in toto". The state government resolved to prepare a memorandum suggesting changes and seek a meeting with Union home minister Amit Shah.Lalduhoma also said that if the Centre did not accept Mizoram's suggestions, the state's lone Lok Sabha MP from the ruling Zoram People's Movement would oppose the Bill in Parliament.Congress’s Mizoram unit organised protests against the proposed amendment, alleging that Christian institutions would be adversely affected because many charitable organisations in the state depend on overseas donations. Former MP Chella Kumar alleged that the BJP was targeting religious and other minorities while exempting the RSS from the law's purview. Church organisations elsewhere have also stepped up their campaign.Special prayer services were held across several churches following a call by the Joint Action Forum on Minorities to observe a National Day of Fasting and Prayer against the Bill.During one such gathering, DMK MP P Wilson compared the asset provisions with the Enemy Property Act and accused the government of targeting minority institutions. "The Enemy Property Act was enacted to snatch the properties of people who left the country after independence. Similarly, the FCRA Bill treats minorities as enemies and is keen on snatching their properties," he said. A nationwide signature campaign and protests were also announced.The Centre has strongly rejected allegations that the amendment targets any particular religion or seeks to curb legitimate charitable work.According to the home ministry, around 16,200 associations received nearly Rs 22,963 crore in foreign contributions during 2024-25. The ministry cites these figures to argue that the FCRA regulates, rather than prohibits, foreign donations. It says organisations engaged in faith-based welfare activities remain eligible to receive foreign funding and that the law applies equally irrespective of religion, community or ideology. The government has also tried to address concerns over places of worship.The Bill requires the designated authority to preserve the religious character of any permanently vested asset, or part of an asset, that is a place of worship.The government says the framework concerns foreign contributions and assets created from them after an organisation’s registration lawfully ends. The Bill, however, provides that an asset created partly with foreign contributions would initially vest wholly in the Authority, although the organisation may apply for the return of any distinct or ascertainable portion funded from domestic sources.The Centre has further defended restrictions on foreign nationals holding key positions in FCRA-registered organisations, arguing that organisations receiving overseas funding should be managed by individuals with a verified connection to India.Likewise, it said requiring central approval before state-level investigations is appropriate because the FCRA is a central law dealing with foreign funding and national security.
Article Summary: The Foreign Contribution Regulation Act, popularly known as FCRA, governs how individuals, trusts, NGOs, associations and companies in India can receive and use money, securities or other contributions from foreign sources. The 2026 Bill proposes a new framework for managing foreign contributions and assets when an organisation’s registration is cancelled, surrendered or ceases.

Article Title: 'Don't cry later': Owaisi makes alliance offer to Akhilesh to oust BJP in UP polls
Article Text:
Brushing off the BJP's "B-team" tag, Owaisi said he does not want the BJP to continue in power.

NEW DELHI: Asaduddin Owaisi , the All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (AIMIM) chief, expressed apparent willingness to tie up with the INDIA bloc, particularly with Akhilesh Yadav 's Samajwadi Party , to take on the ruling BJP in poll-bound Uttar Pradesh.During a rally in Moradabad, the Hyderabad Lok Sabha MP said he was ready to "join hands" or "form an alliance" with the Samajwadi Party, which would be cautious about the offer as both parties reach out to the same voter base in the 403-seat Assembly.Brushing off the BJP's "B-team" tag, Owaisi said he does not want the BJP to continue in power for a third straight term in the state, provided the Samajwadi Party ties up with the AIMIM to avoid a split in votes.However, an alliance with the AIMIM would be a critical call for the Samajwadi Party as it could further consolidate Owaisi's party in the electorally crucial state."I have said this before, and I am saying it again: the Majlis does not want the BJP to form the government again in Uttar Pradesh. I am ready to join hands. I am ready to form an alliance. Today is the time to talk. Don't cry later after the elections are over. We don't want the BJP to come to power again.You say that Owaisi contesting would harm us. I'm ready to fight alongside you," Owaisi said at a rally in Moradabad.Owaisi said the AIMIM's fight was "never against any religion, nor will it ever be. Our fight is for our honour. Article Title: Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann inaugurates 120-bed multi-speciality hospital in Moga
Article Text:
Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann

Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Singh Mann on Saturday inaugurated the 120-bed Capital Hospital in Moga, saying the facility would improve access to advanced healthcare services in the Malwa region. This is a symbol of the growing strength of ' Atmanirbhar Bharat '," he said.PM Modi also referred to the indigenously developed Pinaka Long Range Guided Rocket (LRGR-120), an advanced precision-guided artillery rocket system developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation.The system has a validated strike range of 60 km to 120 km."Behind this success, it is the collective hardwork of our scientists and engineers," he said.The Prime Minister also highlighted the successful flight test of the Khusha Missile, describing it as another milestone in India's expanding indigenous defence capabilities.Later in his address, PM Modi paid homage to the soldiers who fought in the 1999 Kargil War , saying Kargil Vijay Diwas fills every Indian with pride and serves as a reminder of the extraordinary courage displayed by the armed forces."There are certain dates in our lives for which we do not need to look at the calendar. This day fills us with pride and reminds us of the extraordinary courage of our brave soldiers," he said."The towering peaks of Kargil, harsh weather, the challenges posed by the enemy, our soldiers faced every such circumstance, yet their morale was greater than any challenge. They sacrificed everything for protecting the motherland. Today, on Kargil Vijay Diwas, I pay homage to all the brave martyrs and soldiers," he added.PM Modi said today's India not only remembers the sacrifices of its bravehearts but also ensures that their stories reach younger generations.Referring to this year's commemorative events, he said a special Shaurya Vijay Yatra was organised to honour the legacy of the Kargil War. The motorcycle expedition began on July 14 from the National War Memorial in New Delhi and will culminate at the Kargil War Memorial in Dras."Its message is 'One ride, one nation, one salute'. The message of 'Catch The Rain' is very simple: conserve the water right where and when the rain falls. That is why a special nationwide campaign has been underway since July 4. Under this initiative, fresh momentum is being given to rainwater harvesting, groundwater recharge, the rejuvenation of old water bodies, and tree plantation," PM Modi said.He expressed satisfaction over the enthusiastic response received from citizens, local bodies and community organisations, saying the campaign has witnessed widespread participation across different parts of the country."I am delighted to see overwhelming participation from people everywhere -- be it villages or cities, panchayats or social organisations. At some places, silt is being removed from old ponds, while at others, wells and stepwells are being revived. Borewells no longer in use are now serving as channels for groundwater recharge," he added.Highlighting examples from several states, the Prime Minister said large-scale water conservation work has already produced encouraging results.He noted that nearly 1,500 ponds have been built in Madhya Pradesh's Sidhi district, 'Amrit Sarovars' have been restored in Narsinghpur, and Maharashtra's Nashik has significantly enhanced its water storage capacity through the campaign.He also pointed to Andhra Pradesh's Nandyal district, where every gram panchayat joined the initiative and old ponds were revived to restore their utility."Our cities as well are not lagging behind either; encouraging results from this campaign are visible in Korba (Chhattisgarh), Bhubaneswar (Odisha), and Vizianagaram (Andhra Pradesh)," PM Modi said.Urging people to continue contributing to water conservation efforts, the Prime Minister appealed to citizens to take responsibility for preserving water bodies in their neighbourhoods, stressing that every drop of water saved today would benefit future generations."Come, let us also take responsibility for a pond, well, or stepwell in our vicinity -- save every drop of water. Article Title: Nepal eases rules on Indian currency, allows Rs 200 and Rs 500 notes up to Rs 25,000
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Nepal has eased restrictions on the movement of Indian currency, allowing Indian and Nepali citizens to carry Indian Rs 200 and Rs 500 notes issued after November 9, 2016. According to the Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB), the permitted notes can be carried into or taken out of Nepal up to a limit of Rs 25,000 per person.According to news agency PTI, the revised rules permit citizens of both countries to bring the approved currency notes into Nepal, carry them within the country, or take them out, subject to existing regulations.In its latest notice, the NRB clarified that older Indian currency notes issued before the 2016 demonetisation period will continue to remain prohibited in Nepal.The NRB added that only redesigned Indian Rs 500 notes and Rs 200 notes introduced after November 9, 2016, will be permitted under the new arrangement.The central bank had initially published the provision in the Nepal Gazette on February 11. However, it issued another notice on Thursday to clarify the implementation process and address concerns over cross-border currency movement.NRB spokesperson Guru Prasad Paudel said Nepali citizens would not be allowed to bring Indian currency into Nepal from countries other than India.He also clarified that Indian currency taken out of Nepal by Nepali citizens could only be carried to India and not to any third country.The new provision would facilitate Indian tourists visiting Nepal and Nepalese nationals engaged in trade and business with India, said Paudel.The rule change comes after years of restrictions introduced following India’s demonetisation announcement on November 8, 2016, when the old Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 notes were withdrawn from circulation.Following the move, Nepal had restricted the use and movement of those discontinued Indian notes due to concerns over their circulation and financial impact.The latest decision affects cross-border transactions between India and Nepal, which share an open border and extensive economic links. India remains Nepal’s largest trading partner and a key source of tourists, while thousands of Nepali citizens travel to India for work, education and business.The NRB also stated that Nepali citizens and foreign visitors can bring foreign currency worth up to $5,000, or its equivalent in other currencies, into Nepal without filing a customs declaration. Amounts above that threshold must be declared upon arrival.
Article Summary: Nepal has eased restrictions on the movement of Indian currency. Indian and Nepali citizens can carry Indian Rs 200 and Rs 500 notes issued after November 9, 2016. The permitted notes can be carried into or taken out of Nepal up to a limit of Rs 25,000.

Article Title: 'Gratitude to brave soldiers': PM Modi pays tribute to Kargil heroes on 27th Vijay Diwas
